name: Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque
label: Grand Mosque
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Wahat Al Karama' (5 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Wahat Al Karama' (way/391231875): middle (497 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/1635169: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque' (343 m across).
notes: White-marble mosque with 82 domes and a mirror-like reflecting pool.

text.description:
The Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque is the largest mosque in the United Arab Emirates. It was built between 1994 and 2007 and opened in December 2007. It has 82 domes and four minarets of about 107 m. The marble courtyard, with its floral inlay, covers about 17,000 square metres. White marble, long pools and repeating arches make it very easy to photograph.

This map's view is from Wahat Al Karama, a memorial park across the motorway from the mosque. The central circular reflecting pool is the foreground. When the water is calm, the domes and minarets are mirrored in it, with the memorial plaza around you. Guides often name it as the classic panoramic and reflection view from outside the mosque. The mosque is lit at night, and its lighting is designed to follow the phases of the moon. That makes the evening hours especially rewarding.

Arrive early. One guide suggests about two hours before sunset if you want a good spot for blue hour. Another says 30 minutes before sunset works for both daylight and lit-up shots. Haze is common in Abu Dhabi, so a slightly soft skyline is normal.

If you also go inside the mosque grounds, two further views are worth trying. One is the dome and minarets reflected in the long water channel of the main courtyard. The other is the minarets and archways in the pools near the entrance, with a blue-hour sky behind.
text.geographic_location: In Abu Dhabi city. The viewpoint is in Wahat Al Karama, a memorial park and plaza on the opposite side of a busy motorway from the Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Wahat Al Karama in Abu Dhabi by taxi, the free shuttle or the pedestrian bridge. The shuttle runs about every 30 minutes, according to one guide, and the pedestrian bridge is about 15 minutes' walk. Do not cross the motorway on foot. Once you are the mosque is to the south-west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole pool, the plaza and the mosque. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner view. Use the telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the domes and minarets closer, because the mosque is some way off across the road.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Wahat Al Karama (central circular reflecting pool in the memorial plaza, across the motorway from the mosque). The mosque's domes and minarets mirrored in the central pool, with the memorial plaza as a foreground. From here the mosque's domes and minarets are to the south-west, mirrored in the pool with the memorial plaza in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Crouch and hold your phone low, just above the water edge, so the reflection fills the lower half of the picture. Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the middle line so the mosque and its mirror image balance. For a second version, try the same view with the plaza paving as a foreground. If you go into the mosque grounds afterwards, the long courtyard channel and the entrance pools give straight-on reflections of the domes and minarets.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the mosque to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white marble keeps its detail. Wait for the water to settle before you shoot. At dusk, use night mode and keep your elbows tucked in to avoid blur. Try panorama for the full width, moving slowly and steadily.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Arrive about two hours before sunset to claim a spot for blue hour. One guide says 30 minutes before sunset works for both daylight and lit-up views. Haze is common, so clearer evenings give crisper reflections.

text.access_note: Wahat Al Karama is a public park, but the mosque is a place of worship with a modest dress code and its own visiting and photography rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: Louvre Abu Dhabi
label: Louvre Abu Dhabi
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Aptitude Cafe' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Aptitude Café' (node/10829541843): point.
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Louvre Abu Dhabi'.
notes: Museum under a latticed silver dome that casts a 'rain of light'.

text.description:
The Louvre Abu Dhabi is an art museum on Saadiyat Island, designed by the architect Jean Nouvel. Its big white dome, which weighs about 7,000 tonnes and rests on four concrete pillars, seems to float over the buildings and the water beneath it. That makes the museum easy to photograph, because the dome gives the picture a strong shape. The museum covers roughly 24,000 square metres, with about 8,000 square metres of galleries, and it is the largest art museum on the Arabian Peninsula. It can use the Louvre name until 2047 under an agreement between the UAE and France signed in 2007.

From here you can put the cafe terrace in the foreground, with the dome and the waterfront behind it. It is a calmer spot than the crowded area under the dome. Keep the museum in the top half of the frame and let the terrace tables and chairs add a bit of depth.

If you want a second picture, the area under the dome gives a very different shot. Sunlight falls through the lattice onto the courtyard floor and water channels, and there is also a raised platform at the water's edge where a person can pose against the white dome and the sea. Check the official site before you go for what is open and what needs a ticket.
text.geographic_location: On Saadiyat Island, part of the Saadiyat Cultural District in Abu Dhabi, on the waterfront by the museum.
text.directions_text: No public transport stops are listed for this spot, so check a current map or journey planner for the best way to reach Saadiyat Island. Head for the Louvre Abu Dhabi, then walk to Aptitude Cafe, which is just north-east of the museum building. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) so the terrace, the dome and the waterfront all fit in one frame. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner view of the museum. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it for a tighter picture of the dome and its pattern.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Aptitude Cafe (outdoor seating area, facing the museum). The museum's dome and the waterfront in the background, with the cafe's terrace in the foreground. Sit or stand in the outdoor seating area of Aptitude Cafe, facing the museum. From here the dome and the waterfront are behind your foreground, with the cafe terrace in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the dome on the upper line, with the terrace filling the lower third. Keep the horizon level. For something different, the lattice dome overhead and the platform at the water's edge, where someone stands against the white dome and blue sea, make good alternative shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the dome to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white stays bright and detailed instead of washing out against the sky. If you take a picture of a person on the terrace, use portrait mode.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon usually gives softer light on the dome, but check the light on the day, as it changes with the season.

text.access_note: The cafe terrace is part of a commercial venue and the dome area and galleries may have their own access rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: Emirates Palace
label: Emirates Palace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Corniche Beach' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Corniche Beach' (way/1276780607): middle (448 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/30394921: large area 'Emirates Palace' (631 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Grand palace hotel with a huge gold-accented dome and a beachfront.

text.description:
Emirates Palace is a large luxury hotel on Abu Dhabi's western Corniche, now run as the Emirates Palace Mandarin Oriental. It is built in a sandy, desert-inspired colour. It has a central patterned dome and 114 smaller domes, which give the roofline a rhythm that suits a phone camera. The design is strongly symmetrical, so even a quick, straight-on shot looks tidy. The hotel opened in 2005 and has a 1.3 km beach of its own. That beach is private, so the public view is the one to use.

The suggested photo is from Corniche Beach, the public beach. From the eastern section you get a wide skyline view. It takes in the hotel, Etihad Towers and the city's business-district towers, all reflected in the Gulf water. The hotel is some way off along the shore, so it will look small at the default lens (1x). Use the zoom if you want it to be the main subject.

If you go up to the hotel itself, the front is the classic shot. It shows the domed facade with the entrance fountains and the palm-lined approach. Inside, the gold detailing, chandeliers and grand staircase make a quieter shot. Dress modestly, with knees and shoulders covered. Keep it handheld and quick, as security staff pay close attention to photographers. Rules can change, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Emirates Palace stands on West Corniche Road on Abu Dhabi's waterfront, facing the Gulf. The suggested viewpoint is on the public Corniche Beach, further along the shoreline.
text.directions_text: From there the hotel is to the south-west, about 2.7 km away, or roughly 35 minutes on foot along the shore. A taxi to the hotel's West Corniche Road entrance is easier if you want the close-up facade shot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full skyline and water reflections. Then switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the hotel closer. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are at the hotel's entrance and want the whole facade in one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Corniche Beach (eastern section of the beach, looking east toward the hotel). A wide skyline view with the hotel, Etihad Towers and the central business district towers reflected in the Gulf water. The hotel lies to the south-west across the shoreline. From here you see the hotel, Etihad Towers and the central business district towers reflected in the Gulf water.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the water along the lower third, with the skyline above it. Keep the horizon level so the reflections look natural. If you walk to the hotel itself, an alternative is a straight-on shot of the domed facade, with the fountains and palm-lined approach leading the eye in. Inside, a shot of the gold detail or the staircase works well for a quieter picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky or the towers to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the reflections keep their colour. Hold the phone with both hands and take a few shots in a row, because the hotel does not suit tripods. Avoid portrait mode for the skyline, as it can blur the building edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise from the east end of the Corniche is recommended by a guide to Corniche Beach.

text.access_note: Corniche Beach is a public promenade and beach with no photography restrictions. The hotel is a private property with security staff, so check the official site before you go, and dress with knees and shoulders covered.

sources.title: Emirates Palace Mandarin Oriental, Abu Dhabi

name: Qasr Al Watan
label: Qasr Al Watan
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Corniche Road' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '6th Street & Corniche Road' (node/4015832494): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/7232861: large area 'Al-Watan Palace' (630 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Presidential palace with a white granite dome and a large forecourt.

text.description:
Qasr Al Watan is the presidential palace of the United Arab Emirates, and it is one of the easiest buildings in Abu Dhabi to recognise. The façade is white granite and limestone, and the central dome is 37 m across. Construction finished in 2017, and the palace opened to visitors on 11 March 2019. It is still used for state receptions and government meetings, so it is a working building as well as a sight.

From here the white palace sits in the frame with the city skyline and the Arabian Gulf close by. The palace is a good distance away to the west, so it reads as a pale shape against the skyline rather than a close-up. That suits a wide, scenic shot, and the telephoto lens will bring it closer.

If you want a tighter, framed view, the Power of Words sculpture inside the grounds gives a close shot of the palace with the sculpture in the foreground. Entering the grounds needs a ticket, so check the official site before you go. Tripods are restricted, and photographing security personnel or systems is not allowed.
text.geographic_location: Qasr Al Watan stands by the shoreline at the western end of the Corniche in Abu Dhabi.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or station stop is listed for this spot, so from central Abu Dhabi reach Corniche Road by road and approach along the Corniche toward its western end. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the Corniche, the water and the skyline. Then switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the white palace closer without cropping it too tightly. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of foreground, as it will make the palace very small.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Corniche Road (approach from the Corniche toward the western end, where the palace stands by the shoreline). The palace's white façade seen from the Corniche, with the city skyline and Arabian Gulf nearby in the frame. On the approach from the Corniche toward the western end, where the palace stands by the shoreline. The photo shows its white façade with the city skyline and the Arabian Gulf nearby in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the palace on one of the vertical lines, with the skyline and water filling the rest of the frame. Keep the horizon level. For a closer alternative, the Power of Words sculpture inside the grounds frames the palace with the sculpture in the foreground. This needs a ticket, so check the official site before you go.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the palace to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white façade does not wash out. Take a few shots in case of haze or passers-by.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or evening usually gives softer light on the white stone. Light-show times for the palace are reported differently, so check the official site before you go. If you stay after dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a railing or wall.

text.access_note: Corniche Road is a public roadside viewpoint that needs no palace ticket, but entering the palace grounds is ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: From the stand-here point the palace appears small against the skyline because of the distance, so a telephoto lens helps.
Late afternoon or evening light is usually softer on white stone than midday light.
Night mode works better with the phone held steady against a railing or wall.

name: Etihad Towers
label: Etihad Towers
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Observation Deck at 300' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Observation Deck at 300' (node/11942038415): point.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q1371570: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Five curved glass towers on the western Corniche.

text.description: Etihad Towers is a group of five towers on Abu Dhabi's waterfront, standing opposite the Emirates Palace hotel. They hold offices, apartments and a hotel, and the five towers are of different heights. Tower 2 is the tallest, with 74 floors and a height of 305 metres. As of January 2023 it was the fourth tallest building in Abu Dhabi. The complex also appeared in the 2015 film Furious 7. For the best view from the towers themselves, go up to the Observation Deck at 300 in Tower 2. It is fully indoors, and the floor-to-ceiling glass gives a wide sweep over the Corniche, Emirates Palace and the Gulf. It is a ticketed attraction, so check the official site before you go. A phone copes well with this kind of view. Use the ultra-wide lens for the whole panorama, then zoom in on one detail such as the palace or a stretch of coast. Late afternoon into sunset suits it best, as the sky changes colour and the city lights come on below you. If you would rather see the towers from outside, Corniche Beach shows them rising behind the promenade.
text.geographic_location: Etihad Towers stands on Abu Dhabi's waterfront, directly opposite the Emirates Palace hotel, close to the Corniche.
text.directions_text: There are no public transport stops listed for this spot, so plan your own transport from central Abu Dhabi to Etihad Towers, which sit opposite the Emirates Palace hotel. The Observation Deck at 300 is in Tower 2 and is reached from the hotel through a lower-level podium that links the buildings. Follow the signs once you are inside and check the official site before you go. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) to capture the full sweep of the Corniche, Emirates Palace and the Gulf. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of the coastline. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a single detail such as the palace or a stretch of shore.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Observation Deck at 300 (Tower 2, 74th floor, west-facing windows for the towers' Corniche-side view). An indoor panorama from about 300 m up, with the Corniche, Emirates Palace and the Gulf spread out below, and the towers' own curves visible from the surrounding windows. For the elevated view, go up to the Observation Deck at 300 in Tower 2 and use the west-facing windows.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the Corniche coastline along a lower grid line, so the water and the city fill the frame. Try a wide shot first, then a tighter zoomed one. If you would rather photograph the towers from outside, Corniche Beach shows them rising behind the promenade with the Gulf in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Hold the phone close to the glass, without pressing hard, to cut down reflections. Tap on the brightest part of the sky to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly so the sunset colours do not wash out. Try panorama for the full sweep of the coast. After dark, night mode helps with the city lights, so hold the phone steady against your body or a ledge.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into sunset, when the deck is at its busiest and the city lights come on.

text.access_note: The Observation Deck at 300 is a ticketed indoor attraction, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Holding the phone close to the glass helps reduce reflections.
The west-facing windows give the best view of the sunset.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep sunset colours from washing out.
Night mode works best when the phone is held steady.

name: Qasr Al Hosn
label: Qasr Al Hosn
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Qasr Al Hosn' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q7267042: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Oldest stone building in Abu Dhabi, a white fort.

text.description:
Qasr Al Hosn is the oldest stone building in the city of Abu Dhabi. It began in 1761 as a conical watchtower guarding the island's only freshwater well. In 1793 it grew into a small fort and became the home of the ruling Sheikh. A large extension in the late 1930s gave it roughly the shape you see now. It was also painted bright white during renovations between 1976 and 1983, which is why it is often called the White Fort. After a decade of conservation work it reopened in 2018 as a museum and cultural site, and today it sits within the wider Al Hosn complex beside the Abu Dhabi Cultural Foundation.

For a phone photographer, the appeal is the contrast between old and new. The phone icon on the map is under one of the fort's arches. From there you can frame the modern skyscrapers through the old stonework, so both ages of the city appear in one picture. If you want the classic view instead, the watchtower fills the frame well, with its stone walls and textures showing nicely in side light. The Cultural Foundation next door has clean, geometric lines and makes a tidy second subject. Take a few frames at different distances from the arch, because small steps forwards or backwards change how much sky and skyline you include.
text.geographic_location: Qasr Al Hosn stands in Abu Dhabi city, along Rashid Bin Saeed Al Maktoum Street. It is part of the Abu Dhabi Cultural Foundation complex.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Rashid Bin Saeed Al Maktoum Street in Abu Dhabi city. Aim for the Abu Dhabi Cultural Foundation, which is next to the fort. Once inside the fort grounds, walk to one of the arches, which is where the phone icon on the map is. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the skyscrapers framed through the arch. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the arch and courtyard in the picture. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details of the watchtower's stone walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The old stonework forms a frame around the towers, so old and new sit together in one shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the arch up so its sides are straight and the skyline sits in the opening. Keep your phone level so the arch does not lean. For a different shot, step back for a straight-on view of the watchtower, or turn to the Cultural Foundation as a clean modern backdrop.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the skyscrapers to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little. The bright sky outside the arch can otherwise turn the shaded stonework into a dark silhouette, so check the result and nudge the slider until both look right. Leave flash off.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Side light from the sun low in the sky, early or late in the day, brings out the texture of the stone. Midday sun is harsher, so you may need to adjust the exposure more.

text.access_note: Parts of the fort are a ticketed visitor area and opening times vary, so check the official site before you go; rules on flash, tripods and selfie sticks apply inside the interiors.

name: Abrahamic Family House
label: Abrahamic Family House
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'The Forum' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Northwest Forum' (pois); moved 20 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1019914870: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Abrahamic Family House' (295 m across).
notes: Mosque, church and synagogue side by side on Saadiyat Island.

text.description:
The Abrahamic Family House is a group of three houses of worship on Saadiyat Island: the Imam Al-Tayeb Mosque, St. Francis Church and the Moses Ben Maimon Synagogue. They opened together on 16 February 2023. The architect, David Adjaye, built each one as a cube of the same size, 30 metres along each side, with its own details. The three sit at different angles on a shared plinth, which also holds the visitor centre.

That plain geometry is what makes it work on a phone. The cubes are simple, the colonnades, screens and vaults add texture, and the three buildings read as a set when you stand back. The mosque has seven arches, which gives you a pattern to look for.

The Forum is a viewpoint inside the complex that you reach once you arrive. There the thin water channel runs across the floor, and it makes a good leading line towards the timber pillars of the church. It suits a calmer, more abstract picture than the usual postcard view of the three facades. If you want the full set, a second position called The Plinth lets you turn and frame all three houses together. The garden gives a higher view over the roofs and facades.

Photography rules seem to vary from one part of the site to another, so be ready to be asked to stop. Keep your flash off and do not photograph people who are praying.
text.geographic_location: On Saadiyat Island in Abu Dhabi, in the grounds of the interfaith complex that holds a mosque, a church and a synagogue on one shared plinth.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, rail or tram stops listed nearby, so a taxi or other road transport is needed to reach Saadiyat Island. Ask for the Abrahamic Family House. The complex is about 3 km from it, so a short ride is easier. Once there, follow the paths towards The Forum. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) lens for the water channel and the pillars, because it exaggerates the lines. Switch to the default lens (1x) for calmer, tidier compositions. Telephoto (2x-5x) is good for picking out one detail, such as a screen or an arch.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at The Forum (the water channel inside The Forum). Lines of the water channel running across the floor, which can act as leading lines toward the church's timber pillars. Walk or ride to the complex, then stand in The Forum beside the water channel. From here the lines of the channel run across the floor towards the church's timber pillars. For all three houses in one frame, try The Plinth instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Crouch low and hold the phone just above the floor, so the water channel runs from the bottom edge of the picture towards the pillars. Turn on the gridlines and keep the channel level with a grid line. If you want a wider shot, The Plinth lets you frame all three houses together. The garden gives an elevated view over the roofs and facades.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the pillars to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so bright areas do not wash out. Leave the flash off. Avoid Live Photos or panorama if people are walking through your frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Indoors, the light is fairly even at any time of day. For outside shots of the cubes, early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows.

text.access_note: This is a complex of places of worship, so dress modestly and respect any signs. It is described as open to all, but check the official site before you go for current access, booking and photography rules.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light for exterior photos.
Indoor light in The Forum is fairly even through the day.
Modest dress is expected when visiting a place of worship.
Crouching low with the ultra-wide lens exaggerates leading lines.

name: Sheikh Zayed Bridge
label: Sheikh Zayed Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Fairmont Bab Al Bahr' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Fairmont Bab al Bahr' (way/88360599): middle (271 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OSM W407685945 (Sheikh Zayed Bridge): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Sweeping wave-shaped bridge designed by Zaha Hadid.

text.description:
Sheikh Zayed Bridge is a long road bridge with a run of sweeping arches, and it works best as a photograph when you see it from the water's edge rather than from the road. Seen from the waterfront promenade next to the Fairmont Bab Al Bahr hotel, the arches stretch across the frame and curve over the channel. That gives you the classic full-length view. At sunset, or once the bridge lights come on, the arches reflect on the water, which doubles the pattern and makes the picture feel calmer.

The bridge itself is a live highway, so please do not stop or take photos on it. Stay on the public waterfront instead. Two other places are worth a look if you have time. The building called Maqta Fort or Al Maqta'a Museum is said to show the bridge beside the old Maqta crossing, so you can compare the older route with the newer structure; the name varies, so check on the day. The Souk at Qaryat Al Beri frames the arches from the water's edge, with their curves reflected in the channel.

For a phone, the main job is fitting the whole span in and keeping the horizon straight. Turn on the gridlines and line the water up with a horizontal line. Wait for a moment when few people or boats are in the foreground, then take several frames as the light changes, because the reflections can look quite different from one minute to the next.
text.geographic_location: The bridge crosses the water channel in Abu Dhabi.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or station stop is listed for this spot, so the easiest way is likely to be by taxi or other road transport. Ask to be dropped at the Fairmont Bab Al Bahr hotel, then walk onto the public waterfront promenade beside it. Do not walk onto the bridge to take photos. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the arches across the water. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close or want more foreground water. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of a few arches and their reflections.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Fairmont Bab Al Bahr (waterfront promenade next to the hotel). A full-length view of the bridge's arches across the water, best at sunset or when the lights reflect on the channel. From here the full length of the bridge's arches runs across the water to the north-west. Stay on the public promenade, not inside the hotel and not on the bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and set the water's edge along a horizontal line so the horizon stays level. Place the arches on the upper third and leave the lower part for the reflection. If you have time, the building called Maqta Fort or Al Maqta'a Museum (the name varies, so check on the day) is said to show the bridge beside the old Maqta crossing, and the Souk at Qaryat Al Beri frames the arches from the water's edge.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the arches to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour and the lights do not burn out. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on a rail or wall to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset, or the period just after when the bridge lights are on and reflect in the channel.

text.access_note: The waterfront promenade is a public space. Do not stop on the bridge itself because it is a live highway; check current drone rules with the local authorities if you plan to fly one.
claims_not_in_sources: Sunset and evening light on the water usually give the strongest reflections of the arches.
Night mode and resting your arms on a rail or wall will help keep a phone steady in low light.
The promenade next to the hotel is open to the public.
The building name varies (Maqta Fort or Al Maqta'a Museum) and should be checked on the day.

name: Nation Towers
label: Nation Towers
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Corniche Road' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '6th Street & Corniche Road' (node/4015832494): point.

notes: Tall glass towers near Emirates Palace.

text.description:
Nation Towers is a pair of tall towers at the southern end of the Corniche, in Abu Dhabi. One has 65 floors and the other 52. They were completed in 2013 and hold apartments, offices, a shopping mall and the St. Regis hotel. What makes them good for a phone photo is the shape: two slim towers of different heights, linked by a skybridge about 202.5 metres up, joining floors 50 and 54. At its completion, that bridge was the highest skybridge in the world. It gives the skyline a clear focal point that reads well even on a small screen.

The easiest shot is from Corniche Road, near the southern end of the Corniche. From here the towers rise over the waterfront boulevard, with the Gulf and the Corniche walkways in view. That gives you foreground interest and a sense of place. Keep the lines of the walkway or road leading towards the towers, and tilt the phone as little as you can so the buildings don't lean inwards. If you want the pair standing alone against greenery, Bainunah Park is a good alternative viewpoint.
text.geographic_location: Nation Towers stands at the southern end of the Corniche in Abu Dhabi, directly on the waterfront boulevard beside the Gulf.
text.directions_text: Head to the southern end of the Corniche in Abu Dhabi and look for Nation Towers. Walk along the promenade side of the road for the clearest view. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit both towers and the waterfront in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched look. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the skybridge near the top.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Corniche Road (southern end of the Corniche, near the towers). The towers rising over the waterfront boulevard, with the Gulf and Corniche walkways in view. The towers lie to the south-west, rising over the waterfront boulevard, with the Gulf and the Corniche walkways in view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the two towers up with the vertical lines so they stay straight. Hold the phone upright and level, and include a strip of walkway or water at the bottom for depth. For a different angle, try Bainunah Park, where the pair stands out against the greenery.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the tower glass to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour and the towers don't turn pale. Take a few frames in case people walk through the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Mornings and late afternoons usually give softer light and fewer harsh reflections off the glass. Dusk can work well if you switch on night mode and hold the phone steady against a railing or wall.

text.access_note: The viewpoint is on a public road and promenade, but access can change with works or events, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Mornings and late afternoons usually give softer light than midday.
In the morning the sun is roughly behind a photographer looking south-west from the Corniche, lighting the towers' faces.
The Corniche road and promenade near the towers are open to the public.
Night mode works well at dusk if the phone is braced against a railing or wall.

text.description:
Heritage Village has traditional Bedouin tents and palm-frond huts, and it photographs well because of one contrast: the tents and huts in the foreground, with tall city towers rising in the distance behind them. It is a good way to show old and new Abu Dhabi in a single frame, and it is often quieter than the busy waterfront.

The best pictures are taken from inside the village, among the tents and huts. The phone icon on the map marks that spot. Put the low huts or tent fabric close to you, then let the towers sit small in the background. Keep the phone level so the buildings do not lean, and turn on the gridlines to help.

If you want a different view, Heritage Village Beach shows the village's wooden dhows and sandy shore with the skyline across the water. The Corniche Breakwater gives a wide view back over the water, with the village at the edge of the frame.

If craftspeople are working, ask before you photograph them directly. Drones are typically restricted in the area, so plan on phone shots only. Opening days and hours can change, especially during Ramadan and holidays, so check opening hours before you go.
text.geographic_location: Heritage Village sits by the waterfront in Abu Dhabi, with tall towers visible behind the tents and huts.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or station stop is listed for this spot, so use a map app or a ride service and search for Heritage Village by name. Once inside, walk in among the tents and palm-frond huts to reach the phone icon on the map. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the tents or huts and the towers in one frame. Try the ultra-wide (0.5x) for a close, low view of a hut with the sky above. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pull the towers closer and make them look bigger behind the huts.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the photo shows the traditional tents and huts in the foreground, with the tall city towers rising in the distance behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Use the gridlines and place the tents or huts on the lower third, with the towers along the upper line. Crouch slightly to make the foreground look larger. If you want a different view, try Heritage Village Beach for the dhows and skyline, or the Corniche Breakwater for a wide view back across the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tents or huts to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the towers do not wash out. Turn on gridlines to keep verticals straight.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, when the golden hour gives the tents, huts and palm fronds warm tones.

text.access_note: Opening days and hours change during Ramadan and holidays, so check opening hours before you go.

name: Al Bahr Towers
label: Al Bahr Towers
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Al Saada Street' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Sultan Bin Zayed St / Al Jazeera Sports Club' (pois); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/170243985: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Al Bahr Towers' (247 m across).
notes: Twin towers with a moving geometric shading facade.

text.description:
Al Bahr Towers are a pair of glass towers at the eastern entrance to Abu Dhabi City, and they are easy to recognise. The towers' facade is covered by about 2,000 umbrella-like panels in total, which open and close with the strength of the sun. The pattern is inspired by the mashrabiya, the wooden lattice screens used in traditional Arabic buildings. One tower is the headquarters of the Abu Dhabi Investment Council and the other is the head office of Al Hilal Bank. Both rise 29 storeys, about 145 m.

They photograph well because the facade is all repeating geometry. From street level you get strong diagonal lines and a pattern that changes with the light, and the panels move during the day, so a shot in the morning can look quite different from one at sunset. The towers are to the east of it. This is the simplest place to fit the whole building in one frame, and the mashrabiya pattern is clearly visible from here.

Keep your phone level so the tall edges stay straight, and take a few frames at different zoom levels. A wide shot gives you the pair of towers, and a closer one picks out the lattice pattern. These are working offices, so enjoy the view from the street rather than expecting to wander around the buildings.
text.geographic_location: Al Bahr Towers stand at the junction of Al Saada Street and Al Salam Street, at the eastern entrance to Abu Dhabi City.
text.directions_text: From there it is roughly 10 minutes on foot to the towers themselves. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit both towers and some sky, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for close-ups of the lattice pattern.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Al Saada Street. The twin towers from street level as they come into view near the junction with Al Salam Street, with the mashrabiya facade visible. Where the twin towers come into view near the junction with Al Salam Street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line the tall edges of the towers up with the vertical lines, so the buildings don't lean. Frame both towers together first, then move in on the pattern of panels. If you are over on the Corniche side instead, Al Gurm gives a more distant view of the towers across the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright sky doesn't wash out the glass. Take a few frames, as the panels may be in different positions.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The facade is often praised in sunset light, and the panels open and close with the sun, so the look changes through the day. It is worth trying more than one time.

text.access_note: The towers are working offices, best enjoyed from the public street; check the official site before you go if you hope to see more than the outside.
claims_not_in_sources: The facade is often praised for its sunset light (from a travel guide's notes, not the main source).
The ultra-wide lens helps fit tall buildings into the frame from close street level.
The towers are best enjoyed from the public street rather than from inside, as they are office buildings.

name: Capital Gate
label: Capital Gate
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Abu Dhabi National Exhibition Centre' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Premier Inn Abu Dhabi Capital Centre Hotel' (pois); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q1034660: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Skyscraper leaning 18 degrees, often called the Leaning Tower of Abu Dhabi.

text.description:
Capital Gate is a glass skyscraper in Abu Dhabi that leans on purpose. It is designed to tilt 18 degrees to the west, which is more than three times the lean of the Leaning Tower of Pisa. In June 2010 Guinness World Records named it the farthest manmade leaning building. The tower is over 160 metres tall with 35 storeys, and it opened on 21 December 2011. Offices fill much of it, and the Andaz Hotel occupies floors 18 to 33.

It photographs well because it is such an unusual shape, even on a small phone screen. The trick is distance. Standing right at the base makes the lean hard to read, and a guard post can restrict access there. From across the open exhibition grounds you have room to fit the whole tower in one frame. Because the tower leans west and this spot is to its east, the lean points away from you here, so it reads more clearly from a point north or south of the tower. Traffic on the road in front can also spoil close shots.

Keep the tower's top and bottom both in the frame so the whole height of the glass shows. If you want a quieter, more distant view with less clutter in front, Al Qurm Beach is a good alternative.
text.geographic_location: Capital Gate stands in the Capital Centre area of Abu Dhabi, next to the Abu Dhabi National Exhibition Centre, to which it is linked by a bridge. The tower is owned by the Abu Dhabi National Exhibitions Company, which also runs the neighbouring exhibition centre.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stops are listed for this spot, so go by taxi or car to the Abu Dhabi National Exhibition Centre, which is the nearest well-known landmark. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) from where you stand to take in the whole tower. If you are close to the building, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit it all in, but keep the phone level so the walls don't appear to tilt even more. A telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is good for a tighter shot of the glass and the top of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Abu Dhabi National Exhibition Centre (open grounds next to the tower, outside the building's base). The full diagonal of the tower's 18-degree lean against the sky, framed from a distance across the exhibition grounds. The tower is to the west. From here you can see the whole height of the glass tower against the sky, which is easier than fitting it in from its foot. For a clearer view of the lean itself, try a spot north or south of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines to keep the phone level and the tower upright in the frame. Leave some sky around the top. Try one shot with the whole tower and one tighter on the glass facade. If you can get to the north or south side of the tower, the lean is easier to see from there. If you want a calmer, more distant view with little in front of it, Al Qurm Beach is the alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky stays blue and the glass keeps its detail. After dark, use night mode and rest your phone against a wall or railing to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or sunset, when the light picks out the glass facade. The tower is also lit at night.

text.access_note: The exhibition grounds and the area around the tower do not appear to be ticketed, but access right beside the tower can be restricted and there is no public observation deck, so check the official site before you go.

name: Corniche
label: Corniche
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Etihad Towers' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Etihad Towers' (way/1465342507): middle (224 m across).

notes: Waterfront promenade with beaches and a skyline view.

text.description: The Corniche is Abu Dhabi's waterfront promenade, an 8-kilometre sweep along the western side of the main island. It has separate cycle and pedestrian paths, fountains, park areas, cafés, play areas and the Corniche Beach. It photographs well because the whole city skyline sits behind a long, curving stretch of water and lawn, so you can show the promenade, the fountains and the towers in one picture. The Corniche was extended onto reclaimed land between 2002 and 2004. Before the 1970s this was a beach where dhows and ships anchored to unload cargo and passengers. For the classic view, stand in front of Etihad Towers at the western end of the Corniche. From there the arch between the two towers frames the promenade and fountains, with the towers rising behind. If you want a calmer view across the water, the Marina Breakwater shows the skyline with dhows and boats passing in front. The Heritage Village pier is a quieter option, looking back at the Corniche towers across the bay. Both are informal names, so check them on the map. Trees partly hide some spots along the beach, so move a few steps until you have a clear line. In summer the heat is strong, so early morning or after 5 PM is kinder to you and your phone.
text.geographic_location: The Corniche curves along the western side of the main island of Abu Dhabi city, with the Emirates Palace Hotel at its southern end. Marina Mall faces it across the water, reached by a narrow breakwater road.
text.directions_text: No public transport stops are listed for this spot, so navigate to Etihad Towers at the western end of the Corniche using the map. If you would rather start from a well-known landmark, begin at Emirates Palace at the southern end of the Corniche or at Marina Mall, then follow the waterfront. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the arch, promenade and fountains together. Use the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view of the towers. Try the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the skyline from the breakwater or pier.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Etihad Towers (western end of the Corniche, the arch framed between the two towers). The Corniche promenade and fountains framed by the towers, with the towers rising behind. From here the photo shows the Corniche promenade and fountains framed by the arch between the two towers, with the towers rising behind. The long sweep of the Corniche runs away to the north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and centre the gap between the towers so the arch makes a frame. Keep the horizon level and put the fountains or the path in the lower part of the picture. For a different view, the Marina Breakwater gives the skyline across calm water, with dhows and boats in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the bright towers to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour. If people walk through the frame, try a Live Photo and pick the best moment afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon light is best. In summer, early morning or after 5 PM is more comfortable in the heat.

text.access_note: The Corniche is a public waterfront promenade and is free to walk, but check the official site before you go for any restrictions on individual areas.
